newsitem.title: USA: Disney claims success in refining Brazilians.
newsitem.headline: Disney claims success in refining Brazilians.

text.p: Disney World says it has waved its magic wand to make a problem at the Florida theme park disappear -- Brazilians behaving badly.

Tens of thousands of Brazilians visit Disney World in Orlando every year, one of the largest groups of foreigners making the pilgrimage. July and August are peak times with crowds of Brazilians, many of them teen-agers clad in soccer shirts or matching T-shirts, surging through the park.
Staff and American visitors have complained the Brazilians are noisy, boisterous and unruly, a Disney spokeswoman said. So the folks at Disney decided to teach them about manners.

"There were complaints," spokeswoman Vicki Johnson told Reuters. "What we Americans perceive as unusual behavior is normal behavior back in Brazil. The campaign is an effort to make Disney World a better experience for everyone."
She stressed Disney meant no criticism of the Brazilians but wanted to reconcile what seemed to be a misunderstanding between different cultures over things like line jumping.

Patricia Vanmarlen, a Brazilian working for a Miami travel company that sends thousands of Brazilians to Disney World each year, agreed that her compatriots behaved in an unruly way but said it was unfair to pick on them alone.

"My husband is American and he hates the Brazilians at Disney World," she told Reuters. "They push you, drop litter, don't stay in line. But most of the time it's teen-agers. We (Brazilians) go crazy when we are there."
But she added: "You don't have to tell us we're rude. We get offended by that. It's not only Brazilians." She said she welcomed the campaign but felt it should be directed at all nationalities.
Disney World staff also complained that Brazilians were not accustomed to tipping.

Disney launched its campaign this year with a video sent to travel agents in Brazil so they could brief tour groups on how to behave at theme parks, Johnson said. Seminars were held in Brazil with about 2,000 tour operators giving them tips .
Special "leader-training programs" were introduced for guides and Disney recruited more Portuguese-speaking staff.
Asked if it had been a success, Johnson said: "Absolutely ... Even the bus drivers are saying they've noticed the difference."
Staff at Brazil's consulate-general in Miami were not available for comment.
